news.title: Madeira’s Endemic Finch at Risk – Human Feeding Spreads Severe Diseases
news.excerpt: The Madeira finch, one of the island’s most unique endemic birds, is facing serious danger. Tourists feeding wild birds are unintentionally spreading diseases that cause blindness, deformities, and potentially the collapse of the entire population.
content: According to JM‑Madeira, wild finches are appearing in increasing numbers near people along popular hiking routes – especially at the Balcões viewpoint and the Caldeirão Verde trail. Tourists often feed the birds to take photos or videos, unaware that this practice spreads severe diseases among them.

The Madeira finch (Fringilla maderensis) is an endemic species, meaning it lives exclusively on Madeira. It exists nowhere else in the world, making it extremely vulnerable to any external pressure. Experts warn that bread, seed mixes, and biscuits given by tourists transmit infections that lead to blindness, leg and wing deformities, and severe weakening.

The birds’ natural behaviour is also disrupted: they lose their instinctive caution, approach people too closely, and gather in large groups where diseases spread rapidly. Weakened finches become easy prey for predators and often lose the ability to fly.

Conservationists say the situation is already critical. The number of sick finches is rising, and if feeding continues, the long‑term survival of the species may be at risk. Madeira’s birdlife is already threatened by wildfires, habitat loss, and invasive species, so any additional stress can have serious consequences.

Experts urge residents and visitors never to feed wild birds and to warn others who do. Authorities recommend installing warning signs, launching educational campaigns, and strengthening environmental monitoring.

The Madeira finch cannot ask for help. It cannot protest. Its survival depends on whether people understand that nature does not exist for our entertainment. Feeding wild birds is not an act of kindness – it is a slow, silent destruction. Conservationists ask everyone to treat nature with respect and help protect Madeira’s unique wildlife.
